source: Travers, Rolison & Feeney (2016) The time course of conflict on the Cognitive Reflection Test
finding: A mouse-tracking test of default-interventionist versus parallel models on the CRT. People who got the item right were first pulled toward the wrong intuitive option. People who gave the intuitive answer were not pulled toward the right option. This fits default-interventionist ideas and does not fit a parallel model in which the correct answer is always cued.
numbers: N=131 students, 8 CRT-style items, 4-option multiple choice. Conflict items: 36% correct, 58% intuitive, 6% foils. No-conflict items: 80% correct. Correct answers took 27.3 s (SD 16.3) vs 21.0 s (SD 13.4) for intuitive answers, p=.019. Closest cursor approach to the wrong option on correct trials was 49% of display width; to the right option on intuitive trials 55.5%, p<.0001.
quote: participants were initially drawn towards the incorrect (i.e., intuitive) option even when the correct (deliberative) option was ultimately chosen
limits: Students only. Multiple-choice format changes the task. Conflict vs no-conflict response times did not differ overall (t(7.4)=.55) and the bat-and-ball effect was only marginal, so the implicit conflict detection reading is weak here. Lily pad went the opposite way.
agent_relevance: When the fast answer is wrong, the right answer is often not even partly active. A cheap second pass cannot be assumed to already know. Detection of a wrong first answer should come from outside checks (G2, G3).

source: Travers, Rolison & Feeney (2016) The time course of conflict on the Cognitive Reflection Test
finding: In the same study, majority-heuristic people (3-4 of 4 intuitive answers, n=53) and minority-heuristic people (1-2, n=75) showed no difference in any conflict measure. Heavy intuitive responders showed no hidden attraction to the right answer either.
numbers: 128 participants with at least one heuristic answer; all interaction t-values <1, p>.4. Same null with the extreme groups (4 vs 1 heuristic answers), t<1.1, p>.25.
limits: Absence of evidence from a noisy measure (the cursor wandered for up to 60 s).
agent_relevance: Do not assume a model that fails a task still felt the correct option. Its self-reported doubt is not a reliable signal (supports G1: doubt only on an external signal).

source: Bouwmeester et al. (2017) Registered Replication Report: Rand, Greene & Nowak (2012)
finding: Large preregistered replication of the claim that fast decisions make people more cooperative (a famous intuition-is-prosocial result). Under the original type of analysis the effect looked real. Under the intent-to-treat analysis, which keeps random assignment, it was about zero. The authors conclude the original effect came from selection: who obeyed the time limit was not random.
numbers: 21 labs, N=3,596. Intent-to-treat: -0.37 percentage points (95% CI -2.60 to 1.86) vs 8.6 points from the original data. Compliant-only: 10.37 points vs 15.31 in the original. Non-compliance with the time limit: 65.9% in time pressure, 7.5% in forced delay. Heterogeneity Q(20)=16.84, p=.66, I2=2.72%.
quote: consistent with the presence of selection biases and the absence of a causal effect of time pressure on cooperation
limits: One game (public goods, 4 players). It does not refute dual-process theory; it shows that time-pressure manipulations of intuition are weak and confounded by who complies.
agent_relevance: Time pressure is a poor lever to put a mind into System 1. Any test of fast vs slow modes in the agent must use random assignment and keep dropouts in (G7: pay for itself at equal tokens).

source: Rand, Peysakhovich, Kraft-Todd, Newman, Wurzbacher, Nowak & Greene (2014) Social heuristics shape intuitive cooperation
finding: Pooled 15 of the authors' own time-pressure studies and found a positive average effect of speed on cooperation, with large variation between studies. They tied the variation to a moderator: people with more experience of one-shot lab economic games showed a weaker or no effect.
numbers: 15 studies, 6,910 decisions, Feb 2011 to Feb 2013. None of the 15 found a significant negative effect; 6 found a significant positive effect (P<0.05), 2 marginal, 6 non-significant positive. About 20% of decisions broke the time rule.
limits: Self-aggregated by the original group, not independent. The later RRR (b03) did not reproduce the average effect under intent-to-treat. A moderator story that arrived after the main effect weakened.
agent_relevance: Expertise and prior exposure change what the fast response is. A fast mode is not fixed; it is shaped by past tasks. Test a fast first pass per task family, do not assume it is naive.

source: Sprague, Yin, Brockett, Wu, Zhao, Durrett et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
finding: A meta-analysis of over 100 papers plus their own runs on 20 datasets and 14 models. Step-by-step reasoning (the closest LLM analogue of slow deliberation) helps strongly on math, symbolic and logic tasks, and very little elsewhere. On MMLU, CoT gives almost the same accuracy as direct answering unless the question or the answer contains an equals sign.
numbers: Mean CoT gain: symbolic 14.2, math 12.3, logical 6.9 points. Top three categories: 56.9 with CoT vs 45.5 without. All other categories: 56.8 with CoT vs 56.1 without. MATH and GSM8K gains up to 41.6 and 66.9 points for some models.
quote: CoT gives strong performance benefits primarily on tasks involving math or logic, with much smaller gains on other types of tasks
limits: Prompt-based CoT only, mostly 2023-2024 models. CoT costs more compute, so a fair comparison needs matched compute (the authors say so).
agent_relevance: Best direct answer to when to deliberate. Gate the slow path on a task-type signal (symbolic or multi-step computation), not on a general feeling of difficulty. Fits the S0 gate.

source: Sprague, Yin, Brockett, Wu, Zhao, Durrett et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
finding: They split CoT into planning and execution. Most of the gain comes from executing symbolic steps. Even so, a model that writes a plan and hands it to a symbolic solver beats CoT on both steps.
numbers: Plan + tool solver beat plan + CoT solver on average across models on the formal tasks (per-model margins not copied).
limits: Math and formal logic datasets; thin coverage of open-ended tasks.
agent_relevance: For math-like slots, code should do the executing (G1: the program decides, the model fills slots). Slow thinking in text is a weaker substitute for a tool.

source: Chen, Xu, Liang, He, Pang et al. (2025) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Long-reasoning models spend huge effort on trivial questions. Later solution rounds add little accuracy and little new strategy. Overthinking is worse on easy problems. A self-training fix cut tokens without losing accuracy.
numbers: For '2 plus 3', o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. One example produced 13 solutions. Fix on QwQ-32B-Preview: 48.6% fewer output tokens on MATH500 with accuracy kept. Most instances show 2 to 4 solution rounds (76-80% of QwQ cases).
limits: Open o1-like models (QwQ, DeepSeek-R1) and math sets (ASDIV, GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME). The fix needs training, which our scaffold does not do.
agent_relevance: The LLM counterpart of System 2 on an easy item is waste. A code gate that stops after the first verified solution (G3) would save most of the budget. Also supports G1: no scheduled doubt.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo & Griffiths (2025) Mind your step (by step): chain-of-thought can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse
finding: They picked six tasks where deliberation hurts people and tested whether step-by-step reasoning hurts models. In three tasks it did, clearly; in the others effects were mixed. The human-to-model heuristic finds risky cases but is not a perfect predictor.
numbers: Implicit statistical learning (artificial grammar, 4,400 problems): GPT-4o 94.0% direct, 36.3 points worse with CoT; o1-preview 57.7%. Face recognition (6 models) all worse with CoT: GPT-4o 64.0% to 51.2%, Claude 3 Opus 44.0% to 29.6%, Gemini 1.5 Pro 66.0% to 54.6%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 97.8% to 94.8%. Classification with exceptions: CoT needed many more rounds to learn labels.
limits: The authors say models and humans do not share the same processes. Claude 3.5 Sonnet was flat on the grammar task (65.9% vs 67.7%).
agent_relevance: Strong evidence for G1: forced thinking can hurt, and the effect is predictable by task type (pattern, perception, rules with exceptions). Do not apply the slow path to implicit-pattern tasks.

source: Shojaee, Mirzadeh, Alizadeh, Horton, Bengio & Farajtabar (2025) The illusion of thinking
finding: In controlled puzzles (Tower of Hanoi, checkers jumping, river crossing, blocks world), matched pairs of thinking and non-thinking models show three regimes. At low complexity non-thinking models match or beat thinking ones with fewer tokens. At medium complexity thinking helps. At high complexity both collapse to near zero, and thinking models cut their effort near the collapse point.
numbers: Pairs: Claude-3.7-Sonnet with vs without thinking, and DeepSeek R1 vs V3, at equal inference token budget. Complexity set by number of disks, checkers, blocks or crossing elements.
limits: Puzzle domains only. Critics have disputed the collapse claims (output token limits, unsolvable instances); I did not open those replies this session.
agent_relevance: The payoff of slow thinking has an inverted-U shape in difficulty: skip it when easy, use it in the middle, stop where it cannot work. A budget policy needs a stop rule for hopeless cases (G6: still submit a best attempt).

source: Pennycook, Cheyne, Koehler & Fugelsang (2016) Is the cognitive reflection test a measure of both reflection and intuition?
finding: The CRT measures reflection but not intuitiveness. Counting intuitive wrong answers is structurally tied to counting right answers, so it looks like a separate score but is not. After correcting for that, intuitive wrong answers did not track a self-report of faith in intuition.
numbers: N=372 after excluding people who had seen the CRT (of 497). Accuracy: bat-and-ball 30.3%, widgets 30.3%, lily pad 43.2%. Intuitive wrong: 64.9%, 58.4%, 40.8%. Other wrong: 4.8%, 11.3%, 16.1%. Correlation of Faith in Intuition with intuitive-wrong answers r=.04, .06, .02. Cronbach alpha .86 (Need for Cognition), .87 (Faith in Intuition).
limits: Self-report criterion; student sample (about 70% women). Gender gap replicated (men more correct, t(369)=4.39).
agent_relevance: Wrong answers are mostly the single tempting wrong answer (most wrong answers on bat-and-ball and widgets). So the fast wrong answer is predictable, and code can check against a list of known tempting answers for known problem families.

source: Pennycook, Cheyne, Koehler & Fugelsang (2016) Is the cognitive reflection test a measure of both reflection and intuition?
finding: Prior exposure is a strong confound for the CRT. People who had seen the items did better and gave fewer intuitive wrong answers. This contamination problem applies to LLM benchmarks too.
numbers: Experienced vs naive participants: accuracy t(496)=5.53, p<.001; intuitive responses t(496)=5.81, p<.001.
limits: Exposure was self-reported. Training-set leakage is the LLM analogue; no direct test here.
agent_relevance: Treat classic CRT-style items as contaminated for any model. Use novel variants for any claim about fast vs slow behaviour in the agent.

source: Toplak, West & Stanovich (2011) The Cognitive Reflection Test as a predictor of performance on heuristics-and-biases tasks
finding: The CRT predicts a composite of 15 heuristics-and-biases tasks better than intelligence tests, executive-function tasks or thinking-style questionnaires, and adds unique variance after all three are controlled. The authors suggest it captures a tendency toward miserly processing that other tests miss.
numbers: N=346 (251 women). Hierarchical regression on the rational-thinking composite: cognitive ability 17.3% of variance, executive function +5.6%, thinking dispositions +2.1% (p<.05), then CRT +11.2% unique (p<.001). CRT with heuristics-and-biases tasks alone r=.42 (strongest predictor). 55.8% (n=193) solved no CRT item; 6.6% (n=23) solved all three.
limits: Undergraduates, one lab. Correlational, not a training effect. The CRT also carries numeracy, which others separate out (not opened here).
agent_relevance: Individual differences in willingness to check the first answer are separate from raw ability. For the agent, the gate (whether to check) may matter more than the power of the checker.

source: Raoelison & De Neys (2019) Do we de-bias ourselves? The impact of repeated presentation on the bat-and-ball problem
finding: With 50 bat-and-ball style items and no feedback, most people never improved. A small group had a sudden insight and then answered correctly even in the fast first response. Learning came as one jump, not slow drift.
numbers: N=62 (Prolific), preregistered. Two-response paradigm: 5-s deadline with memory load, then untimed. Groups: biased 38 (61%), insight 10 (16%), correct from the start 14 (23%). Insight always before trial 20. Control items: initial 96.6% correct, final 99%. Among wrong standard answers the heuristic answer was 94.9% (first response).
limits: Groups assigned by eye from a plot, not a test. Latency analyses exploratory with huge SDs. Read through a web summary tool, not the PDF. Cannot tell whether people learned the equation or a shortcut such as halving the heuristic answer.
agent_relevance: Repetition without feedback does not de-bias. The agent also needs an external signal (real output or a held-out test) to fix a repeated error (G2).

source: Raoelison, Keime & De Neys (2021) Think slow, then fast: does repeated deliberation boost correct intuitive responding?
finding: A methods check on the two-response paradigm. If people deliberate many times, do their fast answers get better? The order of fast and slow blocks did not change fast-trial accuracy, so the fast answers are not leaked slow answers.
numbers: N=123 (Prolific, mean age 34.9). 120 problems in 10 blocks. Fast blocks capped at 4 s, slow at 25 s. Three groups: fast first, slow first, mixed. Conflict items: slow M=23.5% (SD 40.7) vs fast M=19.9%; the paper notes a 12.7% improvement on slow trials in one condition. 285 of 14,700 trials (1.9%) dropped for missed deadlines.
limits: One problem family (bat-and-ball variants). Accuracy lines read from extracted PDF text; the 12.7% figure applies to a specific condition and I did not confirm which.
agent_relevance: Supports using a fast first answer as a clean probe of the model's default (a first-pass sample), without contamination from later passes.

source: Hoover & Healy (2019) The bat-and-ball problem: stronger evidence in support of a conscious error process
finding: Challenge to the substitution story. People who answered 10 cents recalled the phrase more than much better on the bat-and-ball item than on a control item, which suggests they noticed the relation and still erred, instead of silently swapping the question.
numbers: N=382 online (MTurk 126, Colorado students 128, MTurk 128). Standard item 40.6% correct vs control 96.6% (OR 41.57). Among 227 wrong reasoners: recall of 'more than' 69.7% vs 25.4%; recognition 82.4% vs 30.4%. Confidence 0.889 vs 0.923, p=.047, partial eta2=.02. Response time 34.0 s vs 21.2 s, p<.001, partial eta2=.15. 148 of 227 were fully confident in the wrong answer.
limits: Confidence effects are tiny (eta2 .02 to .03). The first sample had no interference task and sampling stopped after poor memory scores (not a preset rule). Read through a web summary tool, not the PDF.
agent_relevance: A wrong first answer can come with correct encoding of the problem. So restating the problem (S2) does not by itself remove the error; the step that fails is choice of method, not reading.

source: Lawson, Larrick & Soll (2022) When and why people perform mindless math
finding: Numbers in a problem lure people into doing arithmetic when none is needed. The more demanding the numbers, the more mindless math and the fewer correct answers. This is not because people suspect an easy problem is a trap.
numbers: Three preregistered studies, total N=3,193, plus eight supplementary studies N=4,485. Empty box 3x3x3 ft: 70% (N=99) answer 27. Empty hole 3x3x3 ft: 42% say 27 and 34% say 0 (N=101). Study 2 rules out the too-easy-to-be-true explanation.
limits: Authors note the effect may invert at very high numeric demands. Mechanism offered as two possibilities, not tested.
agent_relevance: Surface features (numbers, familiar templates) trigger a procedure. A cheap code check, does the answer depend on any computation at all, is a plausible gate before invoking the slow path.

source: Meyer, Frederick, Burnham, Guevara Pinto, Boyer et al. (2015) Disfluent fonts don't help people solve math problems
finding: Pooled the original disfluent-font result (hard-to-read text makes people think analytically) with 16 replication attempts. No effect on solution rates. Tested ability, format and setting as moderators; none gave a benefit. Disfluency raised response time slightly, with little sign of analytic reasoning.
numbers: Original experiment plus 16 replications. Abstract only; no sample sizes or effect sizes read. Full text blocked by a bot check.
limits: Abstract text only, via a repository page.
agent_relevance: Another cue meant to switch on System 2 that failed to replicate. Prompts like think carefully or awkward formatting should not be assumed to move an LLM; test at equal tokens (G7).

source: Melnikoff & Bargh (2018) The mythical number two
finding: Argues dual-process typologies lump features (speed, intentionality, efficiency, control) that do not co-occur, and that the framework lacks empirical support and is internally incoherent. The strongest rival: continuous or multi-dimensional views.
numbers: Not opened; only the citation and a one-line summary of its thesis from search results.
limits: Full text unavailable this session. Evans and Stanovich (2013, in evidence_a) narrowed the definition partly in reply.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-wire a binary fast/slow switch. Use graded, task-conditional effort (see b05, b07, b09).

source: Keren & Schul (2009) Two is not always better than one: a critical evaluation of two-system theories
finding: A critique that the evidence for two systems is weaker than it looks, because the dichotomy is assumed, not tested, and proposed features fail to line up. A base for the single-process rival.
numbers: Not opened; about 693 citations per OpenAlex.
limits: Title and citation count only; no content read.
agent_relevance: Same as b18: use fast/slow as labels for a gate, not as a claimed mechanism.

source: Bago & De Neys (2019) The smart System 1: evidence for the intuitive nature of correct responding on the bat-and-ball problem
finding: As reported by follow-up papers: many people who finally get bat-and-ball right already gave the right answer in a fast, loaded first response. This challenges the claim that correct reasoning always needs a slow second stage.
numbers: Not opened; the PDF was behind a bot check. Cited by 180 papers per OpenAlex.
limits: Secondhand. Raoelison and De Neys (b13) found such fast-correct people were a minority and often appeared after one insight.
agent_relevance: Where correct routes are practised, the fast pass can be good. The agent could learn fast routes per task family from its own verified successes (needs held-out checks, G3).

source: Rand et al. (2014) Social heuristics shape intuitive cooperation (experience moderator)
finding: The authors give a reason for the shrinking effect: online workers became experts at lab games. Experienced subjects have remodelled their default behaviour in one-shot games, so the fast response is no longer the old social habit.
numbers: Survey of 291 MTurk workers and 118 Harvard lab subjects. Median MTurk worker had done 300 academic studies (20 in the past week) vs 15 total (1 last week) for the lab pool, rank-sum P<0.0001. Economic-game studies: median 10 vs 4. 12 of the 15 studies were run on MTurk. Effect size: nine of 15 studies showed more than a 10% rise in cooperation under time pressure.
limits: The expertise moderator is the authors' own post-hoc story; the RRR (b03) found compliance and selection explained the pattern better. Treat as a competing explanation, not a settled one.
agent_relevance: Practice changes the fast response. If our agent sees the same task family often, its first pass will drift toward the practised route, for good or ill. Log first-pass accuracy per family, not just overall.

source: Bouwmeester et al. (2017) RRR of Rand et al. 2012 (moderators and exclusions)
finding: Secondary analyses removed people who were experienced, who did not comply with the time limit, or who failed the comprehension check. The planned 3 exclusion filters gave broadly the same picture as the primary analysis. The pre-registered rule: if more than 10% did not comply, also report a compliant-only analysis.
numbers: Exclusion subsets: experienced removed n=2,000 left; noncompliant removed leaves n=2,276; noncomprehending leaves n=2,304; all three exclusions leave n=792. Compliance with the limit: 34.1% in time pressure, 92.5% in forced delay. Compliant-only lab heterogeneity Q(20)=29.22, p=.084, I2=33.04%.
limits: Counts are as printed in the report; I did not re-derive which direction each filter removed. A single game and population.
agent_relevance: Shows the danger of conditioning on compliance. When a fast-mode test drops the items the model did not finish on time, the comparison is biased in favour of the fast mode. Count unfinished items as failures.

source: Toplak, West & Stanovich (2011) CRT as predictor (task difficulty and scale)
finding: The 15 heuristics-and-biases tasks varied widely in difficulty. The hardest was the sample-size problem and the easiest the second gambler's-fallacy problem. Most were failed by most people.
numbers: Hardest: sample-size squash problem 15.6% correct. Easiest: second gambler's fallacy 92.2%. None of the other 13 tasks was answered correctly by more than 75%. Composite mean 6.88 (SD 2.32).
limits: Student sample. Same item-level variation shows that biases are separate skills, not one System 1 trait.
agent_relevance: Fast errors differ by task type. The scaffold should keep per-task-family error rates and gate on those, not on one global bias score.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? (outliers and equals-sign test)
finding: The meta-analysis looked for papers whose CoT gains broke the trend. Outliers mostly contained some symbolic reasoning. On non-math MMLU questions, no feature of the question predicted a CoT gain; a simple check for an equals sign in the question or the answer found the items that benefited.
numbers: Category median gains ranked symbolic, math, logical on top. Paper names 10 outlier papers whose CoT deltas broke the trend. Appendix table shows per-model gains, including small or negative ones on some models.
limits: The equals-sign test is a rough proxy tied to MMLU's style. Gains for some models were small or negative on non-symbolic tasks.
agent_relevance: A cheap lexical or structural gate (does the item contain a computation to run) already captures most of the CoT benefit. Build the S0 gate from such features first.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Overthinking of o1-like LLMs (process efficiency)
finding: The authors define outcome efficiency (how much of the output was needed to reach the correct answer) and process efficiency (how much later text added a different strategy). Both are low for o1-like models on easy items. Later solutions made up most of the tokens and added little accuracy or diversity.
numbers: Fix on QwQ-32B-Preview cut tokens by 48.6% on MATH500 with accuracy kept. Solution-round counts: 2 to 4 rounds in 76-80% of QwQ cases and 59-63% of DeepSeek-R1 cases across test sets.
limits: Self-training intervention; not tested prompt-only or scaffold-only. Math test sets only. Efficiency definitions paraphrased from the intro, not from the formulas.
agent_relevance: A measurable stop rule exists: log the index of the first correct solution and see how much later text adds. Our scaffold can measure this before it spends budget on doubt.
